On Ultra NVFP4 with a 4,096-chunk budget, aggregate scores stay within 1.5 percentage points of dense attention on MRCR, LongBench v2, and GraphWalks. RULER sweeps on Nano and Ultra BF16 up to one million tokens show scores within 2.05 percentage points of dense attention with 8-16x fewer KV reads. Serving million-token prompts with 32 concurrent requests and 4K output tokens per request, CISA achieves 2.29x the end-to-end throughput of dense attention using Nemotron 3 Ultra NVFP4 on four NVIDIA B300 GPUs. Selecting fewer chunks increases throughput to 2.61x; in separate GraphWalks evaluations, the smaller budget widens the aggregate score gap from 1.49 to 3.59 percentage points. These results expose a practical quality-speed tradeoff without sparse training.
item.dc:creator: Mohammed Dabbah, Izhak Golan, Oren Tropp, Daniel Afrimi, Vladimir Anisimov, Tomer Asida, Nave Assaf, Ran El-Yaniv, Ido Galil, Yonatan Geifman, Omri Puny, Ido Shahaf, Akhiad Bercovich

item.title: SpecPilot: Autonomous Algorithm Discovery and Systems Optimization for Speculative Decoding
item.description: Speculative decoding accelerates memory-bound LLM decoding with a lightweight drafter, and parallel drafters extend this speedup by drafting a whole block in one forward pass. However, it remains unclear whether their released systems (stock) attain the full speedup that parallel drafting permits. We identify three challenges. First, with one request, each step accepts few tokens but reads every target weight. Second, with batching, per-request verification work roughly halves the speedup over autoregressive (AR) decoding. Third, speculative decoding is deployment-specific, and no universal optimization fits every serving regime, drafter, target model and GPU. To address these challenges, we present SpecPilot, an autonomous agentic loop that discovers algorithms and systems optimizations for each deployment. In each round, a cost model locates the largest gaps between the current system and its ceiling. Parallel agents explore directions and integrate the successful ones. Token forcing checks every output token against stock to detect reward hacking. A structured memory carries validated mechanisms to new rounds and deployments. SpecPilot discovered a general lossless 12-bit weight format, tree verification for hybrid recurrent targets, two-level verification and three batching mechanisms. We evaluate it across four target models, three drafters, two GPU platforms and five benchmarks. Without training or quality loss, it raises the speedup over AR from stock's 4.46$\times$ to 10.87$\times$ with one request, and from 1.94$\times$ to 3.93$\times$ with batching.
item.dc:creator: Kunjun Li, Wenhao Chai, Yihao Liang, Yuezhou Hu, Shuyao Xu, Yi Pan, William X. Zheng, Kannan Ramchandran, Kurt Keutzer, Jiantao Jiao

item.title: Architecture-Aware Mixed Precision for Replica-Exchange Training of Geometry-Aware Neural Operators with Uncertainty Quantification
item.description: Geometry-aware neural operators face substantial computational and memory demands when learning across complex physical domains. We introduce Architecture-Aware Mixed Precision (AA-MP), a replica-exchange training strategy that allocates numerical precision according to replica roles and architecture-specific operations. By retaining FP32 for refinement while selectively employing BF16 for exploration, AA-MP preserves predictive accuracy while improving training efficiency. Across fluid dynamics and three-dimensional structural mechanics benchmarks, AA-MP achieves comparable accuracy to full-precision training over an ensemble of runs, while reducing hot-replica peak GPU memory by 46.9% and training time by up to 25.8%. It also outperforms naive Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP) in memory efficiency and computational cost, with increasing memory advantages at larger model and geometry scales. Ablation studies show that retaining FP32 in the cold-replica is important for predictive accuracy, while additional FP32 operations in the exploratory replica provide limited benefits relative to their computational cost. Finally, conformal prediction for uncertainty calibration shows that AA-MP achieves near-nominal coverage with narrower prediction intervals than the alternatives. These results advance the scalability of geometry-aware scientific machine learning by reducing computational costs without compromising predictive accuracy or uncertainty quantification.
item.dc:creator: Ujin Jeon, Michael Penwarden, Wenqian Chen, Guang Lin

item.title: Attribution-based diagnostics for single-cell foundation models
item.description: Single-cell RNA foundation models (scFMs) are increasingly used for in-silico biological discovery, yet predictive performance alone does not reveal whether their decisions rely on biologically meaningful signals or model-specific shortcuts. We systematically investigate post-hoc attribution of downstream predictions across two tasks: cell-type annotation using pretrained Cell2Sentence and scGPT models, and perturbation prediction using scGPT+STATE in a controlled setting. For cell annotation, we use attribution to assess whether predictions rely on established marker genes and how their relevance varies with model architecture, expression rank, and the surrounding cellular context. For perturbation prediction, we compare attribution patterns with known regulatory ground-truth in a synthetic setting to assess what they reveal about the model's learned computations. Across these tasks, attribution reveals biological feature use, contextual interactions, contributions from different input pathways, learning progression, associations with prediction quality, and potential pitfalls that are not fully captured by standard performance metrics. Experiments with complete and limited regulatory knowledge further demonstrate that conclusions drawn from attribution depend strongly on the choice of biological reference, baseline, and null model. Together, these findings highlight the value of attribution as a flexible post-hoc diagnostic for understanding model behavior, identifying potential issues, and informing the development of scFMs.
